# Celmis

> **Your monitoring already told you something broke. Celmis is what happens next.**
> An alert lands, Celmis already knows which repository that service is and who owns
> it, and an embedded Claude Code session — on your own subscription, inside your own
> installation — edits the code while the runner commits, pushes a branch and opens a
> pull request. On one measured finding that took 220 seconds, from whatever device
> the alert reached first.
>
> Celmis does not watch your services; Grafana or whatever you already run does that.
> This is the part after the alert: the walk from a firing rule to a diff someone can
> review. The loop closes because everything sits on one index — a symbol graph built
> once from your repositories with tree-sitter, no model involved in constructing it.
> That same index also answers questions across repository boundaries, reviews pull
> requests, audits dependencies into a CycloneDX SBOM and a verifiable evidence pack,
> generates documentation, enforces per-repository access rules, and serves eighteen
> tools over MCP. Those are surfaces worth having; none of them is the point on its
> own. It runs on a single machine under `docker compose`, with the model provider of
> your choice behind it.

## Logs, and where the line actually falls

The Celmis application ingests no logs of its own; it starts from the alert your
monitoring already sent, and reads a log file only when a person attaches one to a session
by hand.

The repository, however, ships an **optional observability overlay** —
`docker-compose.observability.yml` — bringing up Prometheus, Loki, Promtail and Grafana.
It is deliberately platform-wide rather than Celmis-only: Promtail tails the Docker
daemon's container logs and labels each stream by container name, so every service on that
host appears in Grafana's Loki explorer, filterable by container. Loki's
`POST /loki/api/v1/push` is a genuine log-ingestion endpoint; it simply belongs to Loki
rather than to Celmis code. Every port binds to 127.0.0.1 and is reached over an SSH
tunnel, because Loki has no authentication of its own.

## What it does not do

It does not claim regulatory compliance on anyone's behalf, and says so in the evidence
pack it generates. It does not watch your services — your existing monitoring does that,
and Celmis starts from what it sends.

Licence: GNU Affero General Public License v3.0, with one exception noted in the
licence file. Source: https://github.com/Celmis-labs/Celmis

## What it does

- **Fix from here** — the named step between a finding and a diff. It starts from a
  production alert or from a dependency finding, opens an embedded Claude Code session
  pre-filled with the repository, the package, both versions and the boundaries of the
  job, and runs on the operator's own Anthropic subscription inside their own
  installation. The session edits the checkout; the Celmis runner commits, pushes a
  branch and opens a pull request. A human reviews and merges — it opens a pull request,
  it does not merge one. Measured once at 220 seconds from start to open PR.
- **Alerts, and fixing from wherever you read them** — a signed per-workspace webhook
  takes alerts from Grafana, whose unified alerting format is parsed as-is, or from
  anything else that can POST JSON. Each alert fans out to the workspace's bound
  channels — Slack, Discord, Google Chat or a plain webhook — and the binding routes it
  by the repository it names, so the card arrives with the code context already
  attached and *Fix from here* starts the session from there. No checkout, no
  terminal, no trusted machine: the work happens inside the installation. The review
  still belongs to a human: it opens a pull request, it does not merge one.
- **Ask the code** — questions answered across several repositories at once, with
  file and line citations on every claim, including call chains that cross a
  repository boundary. The symbol graph itself is built deterministically with
  tree-sitter; no model takes part in constructing it.
- **Pull-request review** — agents read the diff and, where the graph is built,
  who else calls what is being changed, including from another repository.
- **Dependencies, SBOM and evidence** — CycloneDX SBOM plus findings, a timeline
  and a manifest of sha256 digests. Those digests prove the archive is internally
  consistent; on their own they do not prove it is the archive that was exported,
  because the manifest carries no hash of itself and whoever edits a file can
  rewrite its entry. The export returns the manifest's own sha256 in the
  `X-Celmis-Manifest-SHA256` header: publish that where the pack is not, and a
  third party checks against a value that did not travel with the file. That
  check is a separate, dependency-free package: `pip install celmis` then
  `celmis verify pack.zip --manifest-sha256 <hex>`, offline, on any Python from
  3.9, on a machine that has never run Celmis. Celmis does not claim regulatory
  compliance on the operator's behalf.
- **Ask for work across repositories** — every other surface acts on one thing at a
  time. This one takes a sentence: "generate documentation for every service that has
  none", "audit everything under acme-ai not audited in thirty days". The answer to
  the sentence is not the work but the list of repositories it resolves to, with a
  second button under it; scope is re-checked at confirmation, so a repository
  registered in between cannot quietly join a set that said "everything". Automated
  callers are capped and cannot enqueue an unbounded fan-out.
- **Two records of what happened** — an append-only JSONL audit trail (who did what,
  to which repository, when; filterable, CSV-exportable, 90-day default retention)
  and resource-usage history for the installation itself.
- **Spending, and a cap that refuses** — every model call writes a row to a spend
  ledger, giving usage by surface, agent and model. A workspace can set a monthly cap
  that actually blocks further calls rather than only warning. Enforcement is opt-in:
  no cap means unlimited.
- **Run it without the internet** — chat, review and the agent can point at a local
  model server (Ollama, vLLM or llama.cpp); embeddings can too, which is what makes an
  air-gapped install possible.
- **GDPR export and erasure** — a full JSON export of everything keyed to a person
  across every store, and an erasure that deactivates and anonymises. Secrets are
  never included; token records carry metadata only.
- **Access control** — per-repository visibility of none, metadata or code, with
  deny globs that win even at code level, so two teams can share an integration
  without sharing credentials.
- **MCP server** — eighteen tools over the same index, under the same access
  rules, for any MCP client.

## Measured facts

- 197 seconds from `git clone` to six healthy services on a clean server.
- $0.118 per pull request reviewed, on the model it ships with.
- 17th of 50 on the Martian Code Review Bench offline set, under all three judges.
  This measures pull-request review on isolated single-repository pull requests,
  a set with no sibling service for a symbol to have consumers in, so the
  cross-repository work the product is built around is absent from the number.
  Of the 79 findings the benchmark scored false, an audit found 33 were real
  defects the gold set was silent about.
- 23 languages parsed.

## Requirements

Docker 24+ with Compose v2, about 4 GB of free RAM, and an API key for one of
Google Gemini, Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, Groq or Mistral. Postgres and
Qdrant are bundled. Nothing is sent anywhere except the calls the operator
configures: no telemetry, no licence check.
